No. 938
Memorandum Prepared in the Department of State
div.p: Secret
Current Status of Jordan Valley Negotiations
When Ambassador Johnston left the Near East in June, 1954, the position was substantially as follows:

1. Both the Arabs and the Israelis had indicated acceptance of the principle of unified valley development, recognizing the larger benefit to be derived from a comprehensive approach. In general, the attitude on both sides was constructive.

2. No agreements had been reached with either side, Ambassador Johnston having deliberately left the situation as fluid as possible in order to permit further negotiation. However, during the second-round discussions, the positions of the respective parties on main issues had been clarified; and on most of the essential questions there had been indications that differences between the parties could ultimately be reconciled.

3. One of these was the question of using Lake Tiberias as a central storage facility for the Valley. While the Arabs were reluctant to put their water into an Israeli lake, it was understood that they would agree to do so provided the total plan allowed for “safety” storage on the Yarmuk and adequate neutral controls over the distribution of water from Tiberias. Ambassador Johnston indicated that he felt these Arab conditions could be met.

The Israelis were even more reluctant to utilize Tiberias as a central reservoir because they felt that “international supervision” of the Lake would impinge upon Israel’s sovereignty. Their position revealed the political hazard of any undertaking which might be interpreted as a relinquishment of Israel’s control over Tiberias. However, they stated that if and when necessity dictated the use of Tiberias as part of a total valley program, they would be favorably disposed, provided the control mechanisms were not of such a nature as to affect Israel’s sovereignty. Ambassador Johnston indicated that he thought this condition could be met.

(On the question of storage in Tiberias, it might also be said that both sides perceive certain physical arguments in favor of using the Lake. Jordan needs Tiberias water to accommodate its total
area of irrigable land; Israel needs fresh water from the Yarmuk to help compensate for upstream waters which now dilute the saline waters of the Lake itself.)

4. Another question involved the nature of “international supervision” over the valley system. Here the difference in position was essentially one of degree, the Arabs being inclined toward a more elaborate mechanism and the Israelis toward minimal controls on a technical level. Both parties, having accepted the principle of unified valley development, however, were willing to concede that some form of control machinery would be necessary. Ambassador Johnston indicated that he believed a method of control acceptable to both sides could be evolved.

5. Another of the main issues involved Israel’s right to divert water from the basin to other irrigable areas. Arab opposition was very firm on this point and there was no overt concession during the discussions; but Ambassador Johnston received substantial private indications that the Arabs Would ultimately ease their opposition sufficiently to make an agreement possible.

Israel, on this point, was, of course, insistent, claiming that the arbitrary limitation of Israel’s share of the River to the lands inside the basin would deprive her of the right to use those waters more economically and beneficially elsewhere.

Ambassador Johnston had taken the initial position that once a division of the waters was accepted, Israel’s right to use her share where she pleased could not be contested. He maintained this position throughout the discussions.

6. The most difficult question which evolved during the second-round discussions was that of dividing the available waters. The Arabs indicated that they would accept for Jordan an amount approximating that proposed in the main report, plus additional increments for Lebanon and Syria. The Israelis agreed to the Arab proposals for Lebanon and Syria but refused to accept the main figures as the basis of division between Israel and Jordan. Ambassador Johnston, after exploring the question on both sides, indicated that he would, in due course, return with a proposal which might be acceptable on both sides.

Finding the basis for such a water division has therefore been the primary preoccupation of Ambassador Johnston and his staff since his return. During this period, considerable effort has been made to obtain precise information with respect to water availability and needs; and, quite independently of the Johnston mission, land classification surveys in Jordan have progressed virtually to the point of completion. When available as promised by mid-January, Baker/Harza land classification maps will definitively and finally furnish the factor of irrigable areas that can be economically served by Jordan/Yarmuk waters. Unit requirements have been determined by Baker/Harza and confirmed by Criddle. They call for 1260 cms per dunam in areas north of the Wadi Zerka, and 1588 cms per dunam south of the Wadi Zerka, as the requirement for diversion of river water. These quantities make allowances for
losses in transit. They will support the perennial cropping patterns proposed in the UNRWA report on the Valley’s potential.

Also, in general, certain significant developments have occurred since Mr. Johnston’s June visit. Arab interest in the plan is undiminished. Jordan Valley development was advocated by the Lebanese delegate in a speech to the General Assembly. Jordanian interest in reaching an accepted division of the waters has been stimulated by recent Israeli diversions from the lower Jordan. In recent private conversations, the Jordanian Foreign Minister has voiced his desire to see work on the Jordan–Yarmuk put in hand. In Israel, our Embassy has reported that Israeli officials have come to realize that an agreement is not only desirable but necessary if Israel is to proceed with its own water development plans, and escape from its predicament at Jisr Banat Yaqub.

Taken together, these developments appear to indicate a reasonably favorable climate, and it is Ambassador Johnston’s plan to bring his mission to a conclusion during the forthcoming talks in January and February.
In the meantime, Embassies may follow one or several of the following preparatory lines:

1. In Jordan, the Baker/Harza findings as to unit water requirements should be made known through technical channels. At the right time, WRD might plant the idea that the consultative services of Calvin Davis and R. Johns might be useful to Jordan during the Johnston negotiations.

2. Embassy Damascus should use its ingenuity to encourage Syria to be constructive. Syria will most likely get all the water Syria has requested, and Yarmuk power, although the KWHs that Syria might secure are still undertermined.
3. In Egypt, Selim should be advised of the water requirements per dunam indicated above. Continuing support of the plan on both the technical and political levels is of utmost importance.

As to tactics with respect to Ambassador Johnton’s visit, it has been determined that Baker/Harza will submit an interim report to the Jordanians no later than January 15. This will indicate to the Jordanians the areas of land that can be economically served in the Jordan Valley by Jordan–Yarmuk waters and the water requirements necessary for this purpose. Despatch of this information, which will be hand carried to Amman, is timed for January 15. To make it as clear as possible to the Arabs that these figures have not been influenced by discussions with the Israelis, Mr. Johnston will let a week elapse before he follows with his visit to the area. This is now timed for January 23. A stop at an intermediate point, probably Athens, has been fixed to enable conferences to be held between Mr. Johnston and Mr. Labouisse of UNRWA. Thereafter, Mr. Johnston is scheduled to visit Israel from January
26 to February 1 to endeavor to obtain tentative but not final Israel agreement to an allocation of water and Israeli acceptance of a control plan and storage of Arab waters in Lake Tiberias. Then Mr. Johnston will meet with the committee, either in Beirut or Cairo, and explain our proposals for the division of waters and their control. Time would then be allowed for transmission of the views of the Arab committee to the heads of the various Arab governments. Mr. Johnston would call at Beirut, Damascus, Amman and Cairo. The purpose of these calls would be to obtain final acceptance of “heads of agreement” on the political level. If such agreements are secured, Mr. Johnston would return to Israel to secure Israeli agreement to a similar document. Mr. Johnston’s other commitments require him to be in the United States on February 26.

note.p: Drafted, by George Barnes of the Foreign Operations Administration; Oliver L. Troxel, Jr., of the Office of Near Eastern Affairs; and Arthur Z. Gardiner, Politico-Economic Adviser in the Bureau of Near Eastern, South Asian, and African Affairs.
